explanation: The scalp area behind the ear (posterior to the auricle) drains to the occipital lymph nodes, located near the attachment of trapezius at the base of the skull. These nodes also receive drainage from the back of the scalp.
keyConcept: Occipital lymph nodes drain scalp behind the ear

explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3, from cervical plexus) provides sensory innervation to the skin behind the auricle and the parotid region. The auriculotemporal nerve supplies the temple; superficial temporal nerve supplies the scalp above the ear.
keyConcept: Great auricular nerve (C2-C3) provides sensation behind the auricle

explanation: The orbicularis oris is a composite muscle formed by fibers from multiple facial muscles (caninus, trapezius, incisivus superior/inferior) that converge at the modiolus, not a complete circular sphincter. The orbicularis oculi is the true sphincter around the eye.
keyConcept: Orbicularis oris is NOT a complete circular sphincter; it is composite at modiolus

explanation: The buccinator muscle is a muscle of facial expression and is innervated by the buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII). The buccal nerve of V3 provides sensory innervation to the cheek mucosa, not motor function to the muscle.
keyConcept: Buccinator motor supply by facial nerve (CN VII), not mandibular nerve

explanation: The transverse facial artery is a branch of the superficial temporal artery that runs horizontally across the face beneath the zygomatic arch. The supraorbital, supratrochlear, infraorbital, and inferior labial arteries are from the ophthalmic or facial arteries.
keyConcept: Transverse facial artery is branch of superficial temporal artery in the face

explanation: The two frontal bellies of occipitofrontalis are separated from each other by the galea aponeurotica and are joined at the median plane. They originate from the skin of the eyebrow region, are supplied by the supraorbital nerve, and attach to the superior temporal line.
keyConcept: Frontal bellies are separated from each other in the midline

explanation: The buccinator is covered by the mucosa of the cheek (not buccopharyngeal fascia), which is the correct answer making it the false statement. The buccopharyngeal fascia covers the constrictor muscles of the pharynx. The buccinator arises from maxilla, mandible, and pterygomandibular raphe.
keyConcept: Buccinator covered by mucosa, not buccopharyngeal fascia (false statement)

explanation: The lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi (Homer-Wright muscle) is attached to the medial palpebral ligament and the lacrimal fascia. It helps spread tears and is involved in the lacrimal pump mechanism. It is supplied by the facial nerve, not auriculotemporal.
keyConcept: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi attached to medial palpebral ligament, involved in lacrimal pump

explanation: The main sensory supply to the upper lip is the infraorbital nerve (V2 branch), NOT the facial nerve which is motor. The mental nerve supplies the lower lip. The facial nerve provides motor innervation to lip muscles, not sensory.
keyConcept: Upper lip sensory supply is V2 (infraorbital), not facial nerve - FALSE statement

explanation: The platysma (a facial expression muscle in the neck) is supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve. This branch also innervates the orbicularis oris and the lower lip muscles.
keyConcept: Cervical branch of facial nerve supplies platysma

explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) provides sensory innervation to the lower lip via the mental nerve (terminal branch of inferior alveolar nerve). The upper eyelid and lower eyelid are V1/V2 territories; the tip of nose is V1; upper lip is V2.
keyConcept: Mandibular nerve (V3) sensory to lower lip via mental nerve

explanation: The pulse palpable in front of the tragus against the zygomatic arch is from the superficial temporal artery (terminal branch of external carotid). This is a common site for checking pulse and temporal artery biopsy.
keyConcept: Superficial temporal artery pulse palpable anterior to tragus

explanation: The occipital triangle is part of the posterior triangle of the neck, not the anterior triangle. The anterior triangle subdivisions include muscular, carotid, digastric, and submental triangles.
keyConcept: Occipital triangle is in posterior triangle, not anterior triangle - EXCEPTION

explanation: The digastric triangle is bounded by the inferior border of the mandible superiorly (not the hyoid bone), the anterior belly of digastric anteriorly, and the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid posteriorly.
keyConcept: Digastric triangle bounded superiorly by mandible, not hyoid bone - FALSE statement

explanation: The inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle subdivides the posterior triangle into an occipital triangle (above) and a supraclavicular triangle (below). The sternocleidomastoid forms the anterior border; the superior belly of omohyoid is within the anterior triangle.
keyConcept: Inferior belly of omohyoid subdivides posterior triangle into two parts

explanation: The sternocleidomastoid muscle forms the posterior boundary of the carotid triangle. The anterior border is the superior belly of omohyoid; the posterior border is the sternocleidomastoid; the floor is formed by the longus colli, scalene muscles, and levator scapulae.
keyConcept: Sternocleidomastoid forms posterior boundary of carotid triangle

explanation: The floor of the posterior triangle is formed by the levator scapulae, splenius capitis, and scalenus medius muscles, covered by the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia. The investing layer surrounds the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, not forming the floor.
keyConcept: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia is NOT part of floor of posterior triangle - EXCEPTION

explanation: The transverse cutaneous nerve of the neck (from C2-C3, cervical plexus) provides the main cutaneous sensory supply to the anterior triangle of the neck. The great auricular nerve supplies the lateral neck; dorsal rami supply the posterior neck.
keyConcept: Transverse cutaneous nerve of neck (C2-C3) supplies anterior triangle skin sensation

explanation: Six hours after a meal, the brain relies primarily on ketone bodies (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate) produced by the liver from fatty acid oxidation. Glycogen stores are depleted by then; fatty acids cannot cross the blood-brain barrier; muscle protein is a gluconeogenic substrate, not direct fuel.
keyConcept: Six hours post-meal, ketone bodies become the major brain fuel

explanation: The brain absolutely requires both glucose and oxygen at all times. Unlike other organs, the brain cannot use fatty acids (blood-brain barrier restriction) and depends entirely on glucose via GLUT transporters. Ketone bodies can substitute partially during prolonged starvation.
keyConcept: Glucose and oxygen are absolute requirements for brain function at all times

explanation: In fasting, liver glycogen is depleted within 12-18 hours, after which hepatic gluconeogenesis (from lactate, glycerol, and amino acids) becomes the primary source of glucose for the brain. Intestinal absorption is minimal 6 hours post-meal.
keyConcept: Hepatic gluconeogenesis becomes primary glucose source for brain during fasting

explanation: Brain cells take up glucose via GLUT1 (on the blood-brain barrier, constitutive) and GLUT3 (on neurons, high affinity). GLUT2 is in liver and pancreas; GLUT4 is insulin-dependent (muscle/fat); GLUT5 is a fructose transporter; SGLT2 is in kidney.
keyConcept: Brain glucose uptake by GLUT1 (BBB) and GLUT3 (neurons)

explanation: In carcinoid syndrome, the argentaffin (enterochromaffin) cells of the gut overproduce serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) from tryptophan. This causes the characteristic symptoms: diarrhea, flushing, and cardiac valvular fibrosis.
keyConcept: Carcinoid syndrome overproduces serotonin from argentaffin cells

explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyzes the hydroxylation of tyrosine to DOPA, which is the rate-limiting step in catecholamine biosynthesis. This enzyme requires tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactor and is feedback-inhibited by catecholamines.
keyConcept: Tyrosine hydroxylase as rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine biosynthesis

explanation: Glycine, glutamic acid (glutamate), and GABA are the three major amino acid neurotransmitters in the CNS. Glycine is inhibitory in spinal cord; glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter; GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter.
keyConcept: Glycine, glutamate, and GABA as the three major amino acid neurotransmitters

explanation: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as a cofactor for the hydroxylation of dopamine to norepinephrine. The enzyme also contains copper. This is why ascorbate deficiency can impair catecholamine synthesis.
keyConcept: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as cofactor

explanation: Histidine is decarboxylated by histidine decarboxylase to form histamine. This is analogous to other neurotransmitter synthesis (DOPA to dopamine, 5-HTP to serotonin). Histamine is stored in mast cells and brain neurons.
keyConcept: Histidine decarboxylation produces histamine

explanation: Histidine decarboxylation produces histamine, which is a potent vasodilator. Histamine acts on H1 receptors causing vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and bronchoconstriction.
keyConcept: Histidine decarboxylation produces vasodilator histamine

explanation: GABA is produced by decarboxylation of glutamic acid (glutamate) via glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), which requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. This is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.
keyConcept: GABA synthesis from glutamate via GAD requiring PLP (B6) cofactor

explanation: Histidinemia is caused by a deficiency of histidase (histidine ammonia-lyase), which normally converts histidine to urocanic acid. This is a rare autosomal recessive disorder presenting with intellectual disability and speech defects.
keyConcept: Histidase deficiency causes histidinemia (histidine ammonia-lyase)

explanation: Serotonin is synthesized from the essential amino acid tryptophan via hydroxylation (tryptophan hydroxylase) to 5-hydroxytryptophan, then decarboxylation (ALAD) to serotonin (5-HT). Tryptophan hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin.
keyConcept: Serotonin synthesized from tryptophan (not tyrosine or phenylalanine)

explanation: Pheochromocytoma secretes excess catecholamines (epinephrine/norepinephrine), which are metabolized to vanillylmandelic acid (VMA). VMA is measured in 24-hour urine as the primary diagnostic marker for this tumor.
keyConcept: VMA elevated in 24-hour urine with pheochromocytoma

explanation: Carcinoid syndrome (argentaffinoma) overproduces serotonin, which is metabolized to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA). Elevated 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA is the standard diagnostic test for carcinoid syndrome.
keyConcept: 5-HIAA in 24-hour urine is diagnostic for carcinoid syndrome

explanation: Both VMA (from pheochromocytoma, measuring catecholamine catabolism) and 5-HIAA (from carcinoid tumors, measuring serotonin catabolism) serve as tumor markers when measured in 24-hour urine collections.
keyConcept: VMA and 5-HIAA both serve as neuroendocrine tumor markers

explanation: Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD) is required for synthesis of both catecholamines (DOPA to dopamine) and melatonin (5-HTP to serotonin). Dihydrobiopterin reductase is also involved in catecholamine synthesis.
keyConcept: ALAD is common enzyme in both catecholamine and melatonin synthesis pathways

explanation: Alpha-methyl-dopa (methyldopa) decreases blood pressure by acting as a false neurotransmitter: it is converted to methyl-norepinephrine which displaces norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve terminals, reducing sympathetic outflow.
keyConcept: Methyldopa acts as false neurotransmitter displacing norepinephrine to reduce BP

explanation: All statements about amino acid neurotransmitters are correct: glutamate is excitatory, glycine and GABA are inhibitory; glycine constitutes one-third of collagen; glutamic acid is produced from other amino acids; monosodium glutamate is a widely used food additive.
keyConcept: All statements about amino acid neurotransmitters are true: glutamate excitatory, glycine/GABA inhibitory

explanation: Histamine is formed from histidine by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD), which requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. This reaction is analogous to other decarboxylations in neurotransmitter synthesis.
keyConcept: Histidine decarboxylase (ALAD) requires PLP to form histamine from histidine

explanation: Nitric oxide (NO) is synthesized by nitric oxide synthase from the amino acid arginine (not glycine), producing citrulline and NO. NO acts as a gaseous neurotransmitter and vasodilator.
keyConcept: Nitric oxide synthase converts arginine (not glycine) to NO and citrulline

explanation: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting on GABA-A (ionotropic, chloride channel) and GABA-B (metabotropic, G-protein coupled) receptors. It is produced postsynaptically from glutamate by GAD.
keyConcept: GABA is the major postsynaptic inhibitory neurotransmitter in CNS
